q: Who was the first President of the United States?
x: Washington served two terms from 1789 to 1797 and then voluntarily stepped down, setting a precedent that lasted over a century.

q: Which ancient civilization built the pyramids at Giza?
x: The Great Pyramid was finished around 2560 BC and stayed the tallest human-made structure in the world for nearly 4,000 years.

q: In which year did World War II end?
x: Germany surrendered in May 1945 and Japan in August and September, ending a war that involved more than 30 countries.

q: Which famous ocean liner sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg?
x: The Titanic sank on its maiden voyage from Southampton to New York. It carried lifeboats for only about half of the people on board.

q: Which explorer reached the Caribbean in 1492 on a voyage funded by Spain?
x: Columbus was Italian-born and sailed west hoping to reach Asia. He made landfall in the Bahamas on October 12, 1492.

q: Which divided city's wall came down in 1989?
x: The Berlin Wall opened on November 9, 1989. Germany reunified less than a year later, on October 3, 1990.

q: Who became the first emperor of Rome in 27 BC?
x: Born Octavian, he was Julius Caesar's adopted heir. The month of August is named in his honor.

q: Which vast empire was founded by Genghis Khan in the early 1200s?
x: At its height the Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Eastern Europe.

q: Which French leader crowned himself emperor in 1804?
x: At his coronation in Notre-Dame, Napoleon took the crown from the pope's hands and placed it on his own head.

q: In which year was the American Declaration of Independence adopted?
x: Congress approved the final text on July 4, 1776. Most delegates actually signed it about a month later, on August 2.

q: Which ancient Greek city-state was famous for its tough warrior culture?
x: Spartan boys began military training at age seven. Our word "laconic" comes from Laconia, the region around Sparta.

q: Which Egyptian queen joined forces with Mark Antony against Octavian?
x: Cleopatra VII was actually of Greek Macedonian descent and was said to be the first of her dynasty to learn the Egyptian language.

q: Which young pharaoh's nearly intact tomb was found by Howard Carter in 1922?
x: The tomb in the Valley of the Kings held more than 5,000 objects, including a solid gold funeral mask.

q: Who was British Prime Minister for most of World War II?
x: Churchill took office in May 1940. He also won the 1953 Nobel Prize in Literature for his historical and biographical writing.

q: Which dictator led Nazi Germany from 1933 until 1945?
x: Hitler was born in Austria, not Germany. He became chancellor in January 1933 and took his own life in Berlin in April 1945.

q: Which Hawaiian naval base was attacked on December 7, 1941?
x: The surprise attack by Japan led the United States to declare war the next day and enter World War II.

q: Which German monk sparked the Protestant Reformation with his 95 Theses in 1517?
x: The printing press spread Luther's ideas across Europe with astonishing speed, far faster than earlier reform movements.

q: Which battle in 1815 ended Napoleon's rule for good?
x: Napoleon was beaten in present-day Belgium by Wellington and Blucher, then exiled to the remote island of Saint Helena.

q: Which ancient civilization built Machu Picchu high in the Andes?
x: Machu Picchu was built around 1450 as an estate for an Inca emperor and was abandoned about a century later.

q: Which ancient empire built the Colosseum in its capital city?
x: The Colosseum opened in AD 80 and could hold roughly 50,000 spectators, with 80 entrances to speed crowds in and out.

q: Which US president was assassinated in Dallas in 1963?
x: Kennedy was the 35th president and, at age 43 when elected, the youngest person ever chosen for the office.

q: Who was President of the United States during the Civil War?
x: Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863 and is the only president to have held a patent, for a device to lift boats.

q: Which country launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, in 1957?
x: Sputnik was about the size of a beach ball. Its radio beeps were heard around the world and kicked off the space race.

q: Who became the first human to travel into space in 1961?
x: Gagarin's Vostok 1 flight on April 12, 1961 lasted just 108 minutes and made one orbit of Earth.

q: Which brothers made the first powered, controlled airplane flights in 1903?
x: Orville's first flight at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina lasted 12 seconds and covered about 120 feet.

q: Who introduced movable-type printing to Europe around 1450?
x: The Gutenberg Bible, printed in Mainz, was among the first major books produced this way. About 49 copies survive today.

q: Which Roman general crossed the Rubicon River with his army in 49 BC?
x: The act started a civil war. His reported words "the die is cast" have become a phrase for an irreversible decision.

q: Who became the first female Prime Minister of the United Kingdom in 1979?
x: Thatcher won three general elections in a row and served for 11 years, the longest continuous term of the 20th century.

q: Which English king was forced to seal the Magna Carta in 1215?
x: The charter was sealed at Runnymede by rebellious barons and limited the king's power by putting him under the law.

q: Which Spanish conquistador defeated the Aztec Empire in 1521?
x: Cortes landed in Mexico in 1519 with about 500 men and relied on local allies who resented Aztec rule.

q: Which leader championed nonviolent resistance in India's fight for independence?
x: Gandhi's 240-mile Salt March in 1930 protested the British salt tax and drew worldwide attention.

q: What was the name of the ship that carried the Pilgrims to America in 1620?
x: The Mayflower carried about 102 passengers on a voyage of roughly 66 days before landing near Cape Cod.

q: Which devastating plague killed up to a third of Europeans in the 1300s?
x: It spread along trade routes, probably carried by fleas on rats, and returned in waves for centuries.

q: Which French heroine led armies against the English and was nicknamed the Maid of Orleans?
x: She was just a teenager when she helped lift the siege of Orleans in 1429 and was later declared a saint.

q: In which present-day US state was the Battle of the Alamo fought in 1836?
x: The phrase "Remember the Alamo" became a rallying cry, and Texas won independence from Mexico weeks later at San Jacinto.

q: Which Roman city was buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79?
x: Ash preserved the city so well that archaeologists can still see graffiti, bread loaves and street shops from nearly 2,000 years ago.

q: Which Norse explorer reached North America around the year 1000?
x: He named the land Vinland. A Viking settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland confirms the Norse reached North America.

q: In which year did the French Revolution begin?
x: It began with the Estates-General meeting in May 1789 and ended the absolute monarchy that had ruled France for centuries.

q: Which Paris fortress-prison was stormed by a crowd on July 14, 1789?
x: Only seven prisoners were inside, but the fall of the Bastille became the symbol of the Revolution, and July 14 is now France's national day.

q: Which US president led the country through the Great Depression and most of World War II?
x: Roosevelt was elected four times, and the 22nd Amendment was later passed to limit presidents to two terms.

q: At which Washington, D.C. monument did Martin Luther King Jr. give his "I Have a Dream" speech?
x: About 250,000 people gathered for the March on Washington on August 28, 1963. The famous dream passage was partly improvised.

q: Which Venetian merchant-explorer wrote of his travels to the court of Kublai Khan?
x: Marco Polo spent about 24 years away, and his book inspired later explorers, including Columbus, who owned a copy.

q: In which year did World War I begin?
x: The war began in July and August 1914 and lasted four years. It was the first major conflict to use machine guns and tanks on a large scale.

q: Whose assassination in Sarajevo in 1914 triggered World War I?
x: He was heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne. Within about six weeks, a chain of alliances had pulled the major European powers into war.

q: What was the capital of the Inca Empire?
x: Cusco was laid out in the shape of a puma, and many Inca stone walls there fit so tightly that they survived earthquakes.

q: Which British queen reigned from 1837 to 1901?
x: Her 63-year reign, the longest of any British monarch until 2015, gave its name to an entire era.

q: Which English king had six wives?
x: A popular rhyme sums up their fates: divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived.

q: Which Greek philosopher tutored the young Alexander of Macedon?
x: Aristotle taught Alexander from about age 13, and the king later had scientific specimens sent back to his old teacher.

q: Which Portuguese explorer was the first to reach India by sea from Europe, in 1498?
x: His voyage around Africa opened a direct sea route to the spice trade and made Portugal enormously rich.

q: Which US document opens with the words "We the People"?
x: The Constitution was signed in Philadelphia in 1787 and is the oldest written national constitution still in use.

q: Which two Japanese cities were hit by atomic bombs in August 1945?
x: These remain the only two times nuclear weapons have been used in war. Japan announced its surrender days later.

q: Which US president resigned in 1974 because of the Watergate scandal?
x: Nixon is the only US president ever to resign. His successor Gerald Ford had never been elected as president or vice president.

q: What was the name of the Apollo 11 lunar module that landed on the Moon?
x: Armstrong radioed "The Eagle has landed." The command module that stayed in orbit was named Columbia.

q: Who was freed in 1990 after 27 years in prison and became South Africa's president in 1994?
x: Mandela shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with de Klerk and became the first president elected in fully democratic elections.

q: Which empire did Suleiman the Magnificent rule in the 1500s?
x: Suleiman reigned 46 years, expanded his realm into Europe and North Africa, and is also remembered as "the Lawgiver."

q: Which Mesoamerican civilization built the pyramid of Chichen Itza?
x: At the spring and autumn equinoxes, the sun creates a shadow like a snake slithering down the pyramid's staircase.

q: What was the capital city of the Aztec Empire?
x: Built on an island in a lake, it had causeways and floating gardens. Mexico City now stands on its ruins.

q: What was the first permanent English settlement in North America, founded in 1607?
x: Jamestown in Virginia struggled through disease and hunger at first, but it survived thanks in part to tobacco farming.

q: Which British nurse, known as "the Lady with the Lamp," reformed hospital care during the Crimean War?
x: Nightingale was also a pioneering statistician and invented a type of pie chart to show how many soldiers died from preventable disease.

q: Who received the first US patent for the telephone in 1876?
x: Bell's assistant Thomas Watson heard the first telephone words: "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you."

q: Which revolutionary led the Bolsheviks to power in Russia in 1917?
x: Lenin returned to Russia from exile in Switzerland in a sealed train, arriving in Petrograd in April 1917.

q: Which two superpowers were the main rivals in the Cold War?
a: The United States and the Soviet Union
x: They never fought each other directly, but competed through arms races, the space race and proxy wars from about 1947 to 1991.

q: Which US president arranged the Louisiana Purchase in 1803?
x: The purchase from France cost about 15 million dollars and roughly doubled the size of the United States.

q: Which Wonder of the Ancient World stood on the island of Pharos near Alexandria?
x: Built in the 3rd century BC, it was possibly over 100 meters tall and the word for lighthouse in several languages comes from Pharos.

q: Which French king was known as the Sun King?
x: Louis XIV reigned for 72 years, the longest of any major European monarch, and built the Palace of Versailles.

q: Which country did Germany invade on September 1, 1939, starting World War II in Europe?
x: Britain and France declared war on Germany two days later, on September 3.

q: On D-Day in June 1944, Allied troops landed on the beaches of which region of France?
x: Over 150,000 troops crossed the English Channel on the first day in the largest seaborne invasion in history.

q: Which leader proclaimed the People's Republic of China in 1949?
x: Mao announced the new state from Tiananmen Gate in Beijing on October 1, 1949.

q: Who became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean, in 1932?
x: Earhart disappeared in 1937 over the Pacific while attempting to fly around the world, and her fate remains a mystery.

q: Who made the first solo nonstop flight across the Atlantic in 1927?
x: Lindbergh flew the "Spirit of St. Louis" from New York to Paris in about 33.5 hours and won a 25,000-dollar prize.

q: Whose refusal to give up her bus seat in 1955 helped spark the Montgomery bus boycott?
x: The boycott lasted 381 days and ended after the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional.

q: Which woman helped many enslaved people escape north on the Underground Railroad?
x: Tubman escaped slavery herself in 1849 and made about 13 trips back to the South, reportedly never losing a passenger.

q: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the early 1500s?
x: Michelangelo considered himself a sculptor and reportedly resisted the commission, which took about four years.

q: In which year did the Great Fire of London occur?
x: The fire began in a bakery on Pudding Lane and destroyed about 13,000 houses, yet only a handful of deaths were officially recorded.

q: What name is given to the ancient Egyptian system of picture writing?
x: The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, helped scholars finally decipher hieroglyphs after about 1,400 years of silence.

q: Which English queen saw her navy defeat the Spanish Armada in 1588?
x: Elizabeth rallied troops at Tilbury saying she had "the heart and stomach of a king." Storms also helped wreck the Spanish fleet.

q: What was the 1773 protest in which colonists threw tea into Boston Harbor called?
x: Colonists dumped 342 chests of tea to protest taxation without representation, which pushed Britain toward harsher laws and then revolution.

q: In dating years, what do the letters BC stand for?
x: The system was devised by a monk named Dionysius Exiguus around AD 525. There is no year zero between 1 BC and AD 1.

q: Which Italian dictator was known as "Il Duce"?
x: Mussolini founded the Fascist movement and ruled Italy from 1922 until 1943, when the Allied invasion of Sicily led to his removal.

q: In which Dutch city did Anne Frank and her family hide during World War II?
x: The family hid for over two years in a concealed annex above her father's business. Her diary has been translated into over 60 languages.

q: Which event in October 1929 helped trigger the Great Depression?
a: The Wall Street stock market crash
x: Stock prices collapsed over several days around "Black Tuesday," October 29, and the Dow Jones average did not regain its 1929 peak until 1954.

q: Which American scientist developed the first successful polio vaccine in the 1950s?
x: Salk refused to patent the vaccine. When asked who owned it, he reportedly said, "Could you patent the sun?"

q: Which Italian astronomer was tried by the Inquisition in 1633 for supporting a Sun-centered universe?
x: Galileo spent his last years under house arrest, yet his telescope observations of Jupiter's moons transformed astronomy.

q: From which region of Europe did the Vikings come?
x: Vikings from today's Norway, Sweden and Denmark raided and traded from about AD 793 to 1066, reaching Russia, Iceland and North America.

q: Which canal, opened in 1914, linked the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans?
x: Ships crossing it are raised by locks about 26 meters above sea level, saving a journey of thousands of miles around South America.

q: What animals did the Carthaginian general Hannibal famously bring across the Alps to attack Rome?
x: He crossed in 218 BC with a force that included dozens of elephants, though most of them died from the cold and the harsh journey.

q: Ancient Egyptian civilization grew up along the banks of which river?
x: Yearly floods left fertile black silt, and the Egyptians called their land Kemet, meaning "the black land."

q: Which Greek city-state is credited with inventing democracy?
x: Athenian democracy began around 508 BC, but only free adult male citizens could vote, and women and enslaved people were excluded.

q: Who was the last Tsar of Russia?
x: Nicholas II abdicated in March 1917 and the Romanov dynasty, which had ruled since 1613, came to an end.

q: Which ancient Greek poet is credited with composing the Iliad and the Odyssey?
x: The epics were passed down orally before being written, and the Iliad tells of the final weeks of the Trojan War.

q: What was the capital of the Byzantine Empire?
x: The city, founded by Emperor Constantine in AD 330, is now called Istanbul and sits on two continents.

q: Edward Jenner's pioneering vaccine helped humanity eventually wipe out which disease?
x: Jenner tested his idea in 1796 using cowpox. Smallpox was declared eradicated worldwide in 1980.

q: Which American businessman introduced the moving assembly line for cars in 1913?
x: The assembly line cut the time to build a Model T from over 12 hours to about 90 minutes, making cars affordable.

q: Who assassinated President Abraham Lincoln in 1865?
x: Booth was an actor, and the shooting took place at Ford's Theatre in Washington days after the Confederate surrender at Appomattox.

q: Which US space shuttle broke apart shortly after launch in January 1986?
x: The accident, caused by a failed rubber seal in cold weather, led to a 32-month pause in shuttle flights.

q: Which city hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896?
x: The Games were revived by Frenchman Pierre de Coubertin. About 14 nations took part, and the marathon was added in memory of a legendary Greek runner.

q: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin in the 1700s?
x: Britain had coal, iron, capital and colonial markets, and its textile mills and steam engines became models for the world.

q: Which scientist became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, in 1903?
x: Curie won in Physics in 1903 and in Chemistry in 1911, becoming the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

q: Which ship sank on its maiden voyage in 1912 after hitting an iceberg?
x: The Titanic sank in the North Atlantic with more than 1,500 people lost.

q: Which queen of Egypt was linked with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony?
x: Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt.
